about.tool: A broad-edged pen held steeply, at 65° here: hairline stems, thick feet, arms and diagonals down to the right. The scribes turned the pen, about 70° for the uprights and 45° for horizontals and curves; with one angle per hand, 65° keeps the thin stems and thick feet that make the hand, so the curves of O, C, G and S are a little thinner than on the sheet.
about.slant: Upright stems; the curves and diagonals lean.
about.proportions: Capital height about 6½ to 7 nib widths (the 1st-century form about 6). Narrow letters: O, C, E, F, P, T, S about half as wide as high, H, Y and M as wide as high or wider. B, F, H, L and the arms of E and T rise above the top line.
about.features: Every stem begins with a hairline up into its head and ends on a thick wedge foot written as its own stroke, left to right; arms are thick wavy strokes. A has no bar; thin legs end in a foot to the left; thick diagonals end in a small turn. The Romans had no J, U, W or figures (numbers were letters): those forms, and the figures, are written as calligraphers write them in the Rustic manner.
about.history: The everyday book and poster capital of Rome, from the 1st century (painted notices, papyri) to the great Virgil manuscripts of the 4th and 5th centuries such as the Codex Palatinus; used later for titles and headings.
